content: Immune-mediated diabetes, specifically autoimmune type 1 diabetes, represents approximately 5-10% of all diabetes cases. This condition arises due to the immune system's targeted destruction of pancreatic β-cells, which results in a deficiency of insulin production. Genetic predisposition plays a significant role in the development of type 1 diabetes. Specific human leukocyte antigen (HLA) haplotypes, such as HLA-DR and HLA-DQ, are strongly associated with an increased susceptibility to the disease. High-risk alleles include DRB10301 and DQB10201 (commonly referred to as the DR3-DQ2 haplotype) as well as DRB10401 and DQB10302 (known as the DR4-DQ8 haplotype). The presence of autoantibodies can be detected through specific testing, which is particularly useful in identifying individuals at risk for developing type 1 diabetes. This is especially relevant for individuals with a family history of autoimmune diseases, as they are more likely to carry these genetic and immunological markers.
